newsitem.title: UK: UK's Diana to take landmines crusade to Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: UK's Diana to take landmines crusade to Bosnia.

text.p: Britain's Princess Diana is planning to visit Bosnia as part of her crusade against landmines, her office said on Tuesday.

Her intention to visit Bosnia coincided with a flurry of political and diplomatic pressure on the country's factions to hand over war-crime suspects and force a fair division of diplomatic posts by its ethnically split government.

"Diana, Princess of Wales, confirms that she continues to work to draw worldwide attention to the issues affecting victims of anti-personnel landmines and hopes to make a private visit (to Bosnia) in the near future," a statement said.

The 36-year-old princess launched her anti-mine campaign in January with a high profile visit to Angola on behalf of the Red Cross. But the Red Cross said on Tuesday it knew nothing about the planned Bosnia trip.
"If she is going to Bosnia she is not going with the Red Cross. We don't know who she is going with. It is very confusing. We haven't got a clue what is going on," said a British Red Cross spokesman.
Diana's office said only that she was going in "a personal capacity." It said no date had yet been fixed for the visit, but media reports said it could be as early as the end of the week.

Only two weeks ago she was forced to scrap a planned trip to Bosnia for the Red Cross, apparently because of the embarrassment of a possible meeting with Ljiljana Karadzic -- wife of indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic. She is president of the Bosnian Serb Republic's branch of the Red Cross.
The organisation said on Tuesday that it had decided that a visit to Bosnia by the princess would not have been right because of the overall political and security situation.

Britain's Foreign Office said it was studying security risks involved in Diana's private visit, news of which came a day after Britain and other Western countries toughened its policy towards Bosnia over its failure to meet peace treaty deadlines.

"The security of the princess during a visit at this time is obviously paramount and we are undertaking a normal security assessment. In the light of this we will offer the Princess of Wales our advice," a Foreign Office spokesman said.

British troops last month led a swoop on two Serbs suspected of war crimes, angering ultra-nationalist Serbs and provoking retaliatory bombings against international monitors and NATO peacekeeping troops in Bosnia.

Britain on Monday suspended contacts with the Bosnian ambassador to London because Bosnian leaders had failed to meet an August 1 deadline for the joint Moslem-Serb-Croat presidency to agree on the appointment of ambassadors.
The move was backed by the United States, Germany, France, Italy, Sweden and Austria who are concerned by the slowdown in efforts to implement Bosnia's 1995 peace treaty.
Diana's trip to Angola was her first working trip abroad since her divorce in August 1996 from heir to the throne Prince Charles.
Some British parliamentarians accused Diana of meddling in international affairs, but the Angola visit strengthened her desire to be a "queen of hearts" or informal ambassador for Britain.

Her apparent determination to undertake the trip despite the apparent drawbacks follows hostile media coverage of her glitzy holiday in the south of France last month as a guest of the Egyptian-born owner of London's Harrods department store.
